name: Proto-Kra-Dai
region: Probably the coast and hills of southern China (Guangdong, Guangxi), or, on one view, Taiwan
defining_innovation: The reconstructed ancestor of about 90 languages, whose basic vocabulary often matches the last syllable of Austronesian words: Proto-Tai *ta 'eye' beside Austronesian *mata.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Kra-Dai languages are tonal, mostly monosyllabic and isolating, and centuries of contact with Chinese have given them large layers of Chinese vocabulary, including many numerals: Thai *sǎam* 'three' and *sìi* 'four' are Chinese loans. For a long time they were therefore classified with Chinese in Sino-Tibetan. In 1942 Paul Benedict argued instead that their core vocabulary links them with Austronesian ('Austro-Tai'), and Weera Ostapirat later showed regular correspondences in that core.

The homeland is usually placed in southern China, in the hills and coast of Guangdong and Guangxi, around 2000 BCE. The four main branches, Kra, Hlai, Kam-Sui and Tai, divided there before the Tai languages spread southwest into mainland Southeast Asia much later.

chapters.title: Rebuilding the Longer Word
chapters.body:
Modern Kra-Dai words are short, but their ancestors were not. Comparison shows that many roots once had two syllables, or a weak first syllable before a stressed one, and that most branches later dropped the first part. Buyang, a Kra language, still says `ma⁰ ta` for 'eye', where Thai has *taa*; Laha has a similar form. Traces survive inside Tai too. Pittayawat Pittayaporn reconstructs Proto-Tai 'eye' as `*p.ta` and 'water' as `*C̬.nam`, each with a reduced first consonant, and clusters like these are the likely reason why Wuming Zhuang, as recorded by Zhang Junru and colleagues, has `ɣa` 'eye' and `ɣam` 'water' where Thai has *taa* and *náam*.

This matters for two reasons. It explains correspondences that would otherwise look irregular, such as Thai *t* against Zhuang `ɣ`, or Thai *h* in *hǎw* 'louse' against Kam and Buyang *t*. And it makes the comparison with Austronesian possible at all: Austronesian `*mata` 'eye' and `*maCay` 'die' match the Kra-Dai words only once the first syllable is restored. Ostapirat's reconstructions of Proto-Kra-Dai therefore have two syllables, `*maTaː` and `*maTaːj`, but many details, written with capital letters, are still unresolved, and different scholars reconstruct the same roots differently.

turning_points.title: Four branches in southern China
turning_points.description: Kra, Hlai, Kam-Sui and Tai diverge in southern China and on Hainan. The date and the homeland, on the mainland coast or, on Sagart's view, Taiwan, are disputed.

sources.citation: Ostapirat, Weera. 2005. Kra-Dai and Austronesian: Notes on phonological correspondences and vocabulary distribution. In The Peopling of East Asia, ed. Laurent Sagart, Roger Blench & Alicia Sanchez-Mazas. London: RoutledgeCurzon.
Diller, Anthony V. N., Jerold A. Edmondson & Yongxian Luo, eds. 2008. The Tai-Kadai Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Chinese expansion south
turning_points.description: As Chinese states and settlers push into the south, Kra-Dai languages absorb successive layers of Chinese vocabulary, including numerals, which later misled scholars into classifying them as Sino-Tibetan.

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2014. Layers of Chinese loanwords in Proto-Southwestern Tai as evidence for the dating of the spread of Southwestern Tai. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities, Special Issue 20.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Austro-Tai: Kra-Dai is related to Austronesian, perhaps as a branch within it
contested_classifications.evidence_for: Benedict (1942) and Ostapirat (2005) point to regular correspondences in basic vocabulary, where Kra-Dai often matches the final syllable of Austronesian words (*ta* 'eye' : `*mata`; *taay* 'die' : `*m-atay`). Sagart argues Kra-Dai branched off inside Austronesian, from Taiwan. The Austronesian tree records the same proposal.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: The shared words are a limited set, and early borrowing between neighbours on the south China coast could explain them. The structural differences are large, and even supporters disagree on whether Kra-Dai is a sister or a daughter of Austronesian.

sources.citation: Benedict, Paul K. 1942. Thai, Kadai, and Indonesian: A new alignment in Southeastern Asia. American Anthropologist 44: 576–601.
Sagart, Laurent. 2004. The higher phylogeny of Austronesian and the position of Tai-Kadai. Oceanic Linguistics 43(2).

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Tai as Sino-Tibetan: Thai and its relatives belong with Chinese
contested_classifications.evidence_for: Tai and Chinese share tone systems, monosyllabic words and a large vocabulary, including numerals. The older Western and Chinese classifications put them together.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: The shared vocabulary is borrowed in datable layers, and the tones developed in parallel and later, as they did in Vietnamese. The core vocabulary points elsewhere. Almost all specialists now treat Kra-Dai as a separate family.

sources.citation: Benedict, Paul K. 1942. Thai, Kadai, and Indonesian: A new alignment in Southeastern Asia. American Anthropologist 44: 576–601.

speakers.note: About two-thirds speak Thai, Lao or Isan; the total also includes Central Tai (Tày, Nùng, Southern Zhuang) and Be of Hainan, which have no branch of their own here.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Diller, Anthony V. N., Jerold A. Edmondson & Yongxian Luo, eds. 2008. The Tai-Kadai Languages. London: Routledge.
